edges: Walvin: after the quota ended in 1974, sugar prices jumped and fluctuated, and the soft-drink makers looked for an alternative sweetener — corn syrup.
Walvin: the 1973 Farm Bill made corn syrup cheap, and Coca-Cola switched to it in 1980 and 1985.
Walvin: with cheap corn sweetener Coca-Cola increased the sizes of its bottles and cans, and per-head soft-drink consumption rose from 28.7 to 36.9 gallons in 1985–98.
Walvin: Americans’ sweetener consumption rose from just over 100 lb in 1950 to 153 lb in 2000, soft drinks being a large part.
Walvin: McDonald’s ‘large’ (1972) and ‘supersized’ (1994) went hand in hand with Coke’s bigger servings.
Walvin: Coke’s growth followed the rise of McDonald’s and other fast-food chains; by 2000 McDonald’s was Coca-Cola’s biggest customer.
Walvin ties eating out and the microwave kitchen to the packaged food that carried the added sweeteners.
Walvin: food scientists hunting for the ‘bliss point’ were designing sweet products for children, such as cereals.
Walvin: research into taste and sweetness provided food and drink makers with opportunities and ways to appeal to children in advertising.
Smith: the FDA’s cyclamate ban of 1970 and saccharin’s moratorium left aspartame to become the main diet sweetener.
Smith: studies of saccharin’s safety, from 1977 to the lifting of the ban in 1991, are part of the long debate over sugar substitutes.
Smith pairs Yudkin’s 1972 book with Duffy’s Sugar Blues of 1975 as the public critics of sugar before the medical establishment’s turn.
Walvin: critics of sugar like Yudkin were belittled while the sugar interests’ research funded in 1967 pointed to fat — exposed in 2016.
Walvin treats the 2016 revelations as the background against which the AHA and others’ sugar limits were set in 2009 and 2015.
The AHA’s 2009 alarm at a ‘worldwide pandemic’ and the Lancet’s 2011 figures belong to the same body of evidence in Walvin’s and Smith’s accounts.
Smith’s Lancet figures and Walvin’s WHO 2015 figures are two measures of the global rise in obesity since 1980.
Walvin: childhood obesity in Britain and the USA is the starker form of the global rise, with 60 per cent more since 1990.
Smith’s Liquid Candy report and the Royal College of Surgeons’ 2005 statement both concern children’s health from soft drinks and sugar.
Walvin: the food industry’s fear of tobacco-style liability suits came as obesity, and sugar’s role in it, were widely compared to tobacco in 2004.
Walvin: Jamie Oliver’s ‘next tobacco’ echoes the comparison that American industry had been afraid of since 2004.
Walvin: the 2015 PHE report forced the British Government’s hand and led to the soft-drinks levy of 2018.
Walvin: after the PHE report’s publication in October 2015 journalists and celebrities such as Jamie Oliver joined the attack on sugar.
Walvin: Mexico’s tax was one of the precedents that led other places, including Britain, to consider sugar taxes.
Walvin: the sugar taxes already introduced elsewhere were the first argument for a British tax.
The WHO guideline of 2015 and the British levy of 2016 belong to the same year’s push for lower sugar intake.
Walvin: in the summer of 2016, with the tax announced, Coca-Cola’s ‘Zero Sugar’ advertisements bombarded British viewers.
Walvin: Coca-Cola, already in over 200 countries, added bottled water in 1999 when tap-water consumption fell.
The EU’s sugar quotas that ended in 2017 were at odds with its WTO export commitments, the subject of Walvin’s complaint about farm subsidies.
Walvin: subsidies went to major corporations, among them the transnational sugar companies of Europe, in the same global food system.
The oil shocks of the 1970s led Brazil to launch Proálcool in 1975.
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 removed Cuban sugar’s main buyer, halving output.
Walvin ties the Florida cane workers’ treatment in the 1980s to a boom in sugar for the American market.
Walvin treats the rises in British and American soft-drink consumption as one story.
Smith treats energy drinks like Red Bull and the sugar substitutes as the new products of the post-war food industry.
